kinds.instruction: Do not propose. You are shown both the documented rules and the source. Read this cycle's executions beside the proposals: for each expectation that failed, say whether the proposer misread the rule, or the rule as written and the code part company; quote the rule's words and name the line of code. Say which failures matter and what a proposer should try next. Cite blocks by id. A prediction beside each proposal says what a reader of the code expected; where the expectation from the rule and the prediction from the code disagree, and the machine sided with one, say which reading was wrong and why.

kinds.instruction: Do not propose. You are shown the source of the checks and ONE proposal: an input, a rewritten text, and the proposer's expectation, which was written from the documented rules without the code. Read the code, not the proposer's expectation, and commit what the code will do on this pair: will the kernel's answer on the rewritten text differ from its answer on the input ('moves') or not ('unchanged')? Trace the code on both texts in the body. The commitments are a STRING whose content is JSON of the form {"proposal": "<the 16-character id of the proposal>", "expect": "moves" or "unchanged", "trace": "<one sentence: which line decides it>"}.

kinds.instruction: You are shown the documented rules of the checks, not their code. Write ONE test pair: an input and your own rewritten version of it, and say what the RULE, read as written, says the check's answer ought to do: move ('moves') or stay ('unchanged'). Your expectation comes from the rule's words alone. Aim for the cases the wording leaves open or decides by a clause a reader could miss: what counts as inside a fence, what counts as top-level, what prose around or inside a fence does, what a second object does, what the refusal list's order does. Your kernel is conformance.kernel.grounding or conformance.kernel.span-occurs. For the grounding kernels the input is one JSON object with the fields value, span and document, written out as a string; a line break inside a field is written as \n. The commitments are a STRING whose content is JSON of the form {"kernel": "<id>", "input": "<the input text>", "rewritten": "<your rewritten text>", "expect": "moves" or "unchanged", "rewrite": "<one sentence naming what you changed>"}. The input and the rewritten text are instances written out in full, never descriptions. Do not repeat a pair shown among the earlier proposals.

port_types.header: The documented rules of the checks

problem: The checks under test are the conformance harness's own functions. Most seats are shown only their documented rules, not their code: how the harness recovers a JSON object from a reply, whether it had to recover it from prose, its response verdict, its refusal-phrase check, and its grounding matcher. The question: is there an input and a rewrite of it on which the rule, read as written, says one thing and the check, run by machine, does another? The executor runs the check on both texts and records what its answer did; nothing here decides anything, the record shows where a reading and the machine parted.
